cells.tense: The sense of what matters is steady and being acted on right now
cells.ask: Say one fair thing today that would normally go unsaid
cells.core:
You're steady where it counts. You can tell what deserves attention here without grinding through the analysis first, and you move on it while it's still true — the sensing and the doing run together, which is why people around you lean on your read. That's going well, and it's also why less of it gets said out loud than should.

What this steadiness can feed next is fairness traveling both ways. Look for one place where giving has gone one-directional, and say the fair thing once — let it be answered rather than audited. If you're wrong about the situation, saying it still shows you what's moving.

cells.tense: You're bracing at a version of next month that hasn't arrived
cells.ask: Name one ending you keep walking around, out loud, once
cells.core:
When you can see this far ahead, you start rearranging before it's real — cutting, planning, getting the next thing ready while the present one stands. You'd call that being prepared. It's also what keeps you out of the part of the work that only moves when the ending is allowed to be one and the people in it get to be in it with you.

Say one ending you can already sense, in the plainest words you have, today. The floor under you gets firmer when it stops being one you're still building.

cells.tense: You're at a door the room has already closed behind you
cells.ask: Carry one kept-past-its-season object out, or cancel one such commitment
cells.core:
When a chapter finishes and the room stays the same, the sense of what matters now has little to work on. You can still read a room; the trouble is the room you're reading is the one that's gone, so the sense has nothing current to land on.

This comes back through movement, not reflection. Pick one thing kept past its season — an item, a standing date, a task nobody needs — and take it out of the room or say the finished sentence to someone. You don't have to feel ready; one real move pulls the next into view, and you'll find you still know how to choose.

cells.tense: The pen is down in a room where you're already reading the situation
cells.ask: Make one decision today and write the reason you actually used
cells.core:
Watch how things stay standing around you and it isn't luck. You weigh what will hold and what will break, then you pick — a clean read of a room, doing its work whether or not anyone names it, including you. That's what stewardship looks like here, and it's running quietly in everything from the schedule to whose complaint gets answered first.

On your next decision, write down the reason you actually used — the real one, not the tidy one — and keep it. If the read turns out wrong, you've still learned how you think, and the next call comes quicker.
